title: Young MC Says Freedom 250 Gig Was a ‘Bait-and-Switch’: ‘I Had No Clue It Was Trump-Backed’
summary: When Young MC’s agent offered him a slot at a D.C. concert called Freedom 250, the “Bust a Move” rapper saw it as a chance to honor his late friend Rob Base, who had died just days earlier. But within hours of the lineup being posted on Instagram, Young MC was fielding furious comments calling him a “MAGA douchebag.” He had no idea the event was tied to the Trump administration. “I had no clue it was considered a ‘Trump-backed’ event, so that was new to me,” Young MC told Rolling Stone. “My whole thing was ‘tell me what the event is, what it’s about, who you are, and then give me the choice of whether I want to do the event or not.’ I was never given that choice. I was told one thing and then it was a bait-and-switch.” The concert, billed as part of “The Great American State Fair,” featured a slate of ’90s nostalgia acts including Vanilla Ice, Milli Vanilli, and C&C Music Factory. But after SPIN magazine described it as “Trump-backed,” artists began distancing themselves. Morris Day and the Time flatly denied involvement, and Freedom Williams of C&C Music Factory also backed out. Young MC, who identifies as a political independent, said he performs for audiences of all beliefs but draws the line at covert partisanship. “When an event is presented to an artist they’re booked on as nonpolitical and nonpartisan, and then turns around and becomes hyper-partisan like it’s a rally, that’s when I have a problem.” He emphasized that music is his escape from divisiveness: “I’m not asking people who they vote for when they come to my show.” The rapper’s transparency won over many fans, and even the commenter who insulted him apologized. For Young MC, the incident was a reminder that artists deserve to know what they’re signing up for — especially when the stakes are more than just a paycheck.
why_it_matters: This incident highlights how performers can be misled into associating with political causes, violating their personal boundaries and risking their fan base. It underscores the need for clear communication and transparency in event booking, especially when partisan politics can polarize audiences.

background_read: The 'Great American State Fair' was a proposed event tied to the Trump administration, modeled on state fairs with concerts and patriotic displays, though it was later scaled back.
Young MC (Marvin Young) was one of the first hip-hop artists to win a Grammy for Best Rap Performance (1990) with the crossover hit 'Bust a Move,' which bridged rock and hip-hop audiences.

Rob Base, part of the duo Rob Base and DJ E-Z Rock, was famous for the 1988 anthem 'It Takes Two,' a staple of dance floors and sports arenas; he died just days before the Freedom 250 lineup was announced.
SPIN magazine (a music publication founded in 1985) first labeled the event as 'Trump-backed,' triggering a wave of artist pullouts.

C&C Music Factory's Freedom Williams also withdrew, and Morris Day and the Time (a funk band from Prince's Minneapolis circle) flatly denied involvement, showing how quickly nostalgia acts can be entangled in politics.

perspectives.description: Young MC's refusal to go along with a deceptive booking earned him respect, showing that honesty can strengthen fan loyalty. His openness about what happened turned a potential scandal into a moment of trust.

The organizers misrepresented the gig as nonpolitical, potentially harming artists' reputations and exploiting their goodwill for political gain. This raises ethical red flags about how events are presented to talent.

The use of nostalgia acts to draw crowds to political rallies is a growing trend, blurring the line between nonpartisan entertainment and partisan messaging. Artists may not realize they are being used as draws for a political base.

Artists may now insist on clear political-disclosure clauses in performance agreements, and fans may become more vigilant about vetting the events they support. The incident could lead to industry-wide discussions about informed consent in bookings.
